craft_claim: Distrust is an active attributional stance, not passive negativity: suspicion prompts motive-hunting, distrust coexists with trust as a separate vigilance construct, and audiences spontaneously monitor persuasive intent — so the cynical voice dramatizes the reading of stated motives.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 70(6):1164-1184
supporting_evidence.note: Induced suspicion led perceivers to search for ulterior and situational causes and reduced the correspondence bias; suspicion changes what causes people attribute, not merely how they feel.

Trust and distrust are argued to be related but separate constructs that can coexist; distrust is a confident orientation toward untrustworthy conduct — a vigilance posture the cynical voice performs.

The Persuasion Knowledge Model holds that people monitor messages and agents for persuasive intent and cope with a learned repertoire that can include resistance; readers already arrive suspicious of being worked on.

counterevidence.note: Section G 'The cynic as unreliable reasoner': because suspicion reallocates attribution, a cynically reasoning narrator can be systematically wrong and see ulterior motives where none exist; without a built-in gap between the narrator's deflations and reality the voice simply teaches the reader to distrust the narrator.

scope: Narrator or viewpoint speech in which stated motives are foregrounded: institutional narration, character interiority, essay and copy addressed to a skeptical reader.
exceptions: Suspicion is fallible and costly: over-attribution of ulterior motives distorts judgment, so a cynical reasoner can be an unreliable one (cross-link clm-unreliable-narration).
Naive or trust-first narration remains the default for most protagonists; the stance must be earned by the text's world.
